content: The study titled Efavirenz/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir DF for Initial Treatment of HIV-1 Infection: Analysis of Week 144 Results published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2014 (Volume 65, Issue 3, Pages e118–e121) evaluates the long-term efficacy and safety of this combination therapy in treatment-naïve HIV-1-infected individuals. The ENCORE1 Study Group conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, non-inferiority trial comparing the efficacy of a reduced 400 mg dose of efavirenz to the standard 600 mg dose in antiretroviral-naïve adults with HIV infection. The results, published in The Lancet in 2014 (Volume 383, Issue 9927, Pages 1474–1482), demonstrated that the lower dose was non-inferior in terms of virological suppression, with a potentially improved safety profile. McCormack PL reviewed the use of dolutegravir in managing HIV-1 infection in adolescents and adults, highlighting its efficacy, tolerability, and role in treatment regimens. This review was published in Drugs in 2014 (Volume 74, Pages 1241–1252). Trevino et al. explored the use of dolutegravir for treating HIV-2 infection, emphasizing its effectiveness in this less common form of HIV. Their findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Virology in 2015 (Volume 64, Pages 12–15). Descamps et al. reported on the use of dolutegravir in HIV-2-infected patients with resistance to first-line integrase inhibitors. This study, part of the French named patient program, was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2015 (Volume 60, Issue 10, Pages 1521–1527). Hill et al. conducted a systematic review of 12 pharmacokinetic studies to assess the time-dependent drug interaction between rifampicin and efavirenz. The findings were presented at the International AIDS Conference in Melbourne, Australia, in July 2014 (Abstract MOPE040). Dooley et al. investigated the pharmacokinetics of efavirenz and its use in treating HIV-1 among pregnant women with and without tuberculosis co-infection. Their study, published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2015 (Volume 211, Issue 2, Pages 197–205), provided insights into dosing adjustments in this population. Dooley et al. also conducted a Phase 1 study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of dolutegravir administered twice daily with rifampin or once daily with rifabutin in healthy subjects. The results were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2013 (Volume 62, Issue 1, Pages 21–27). Olagunju et al. examined the pharmacogenetics of pregnancy-induced changes in efavirenz pharmacokinetics, with their findings published in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics in 2015 (Volume 97, Issue 3, Pages 298–306). Hill et al. addressed whether pregnancy affects the pharmacokinetics of efavirenz in their study published in AIDS in 2014 (Volume 28, Issue 10, Pages 1542–1543). Song et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of dolutegravir when co-administered with mineral supplements in healthy adult subjects. Their findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2015 (Volume 55, Issue 5, Pages 490–496). The National Institutes of Health conducted an open-label study comparing dolutegravir and efavirenz for HIV-tuberculosis co-infection. Details of the study can be accessed via ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02178592, accessed October 31, 2015). The National Institutes of Health also initiated a pilot study (DOLPHIN 1) to evaluate the safety and pharmacokinetics of dolutegravir in pregnant HIV-infected mothers and their neonates. This study is available on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02245022, accessed October 31, 2015). The Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) provided global forecasts of antiretroviral demand for 2014–2018 and projections for new formulations for 2015–2024. The report also included updates on hepatitis B and C. The document is accessible via the World Health Organization's website (accessed February 8, 2016). Van Leth et al. compared first-line antiretroviral therapy regimens including nevirapine, efavirenz, or both drugs, combined with stavudine and lamivudine, in a randomized open-label trial (2NN Study). The results were published in The Lancet in 2004 (Volume 363, Issue 9417, Pages 1253–1263). Jamisse et al. investigated antiretroviral-associated toxicity in HIV-1-seropositive pregnant women in Mozambique receiving nevirapine-based regimens. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2007 (Volume 44, Issue 4, Pages 371–376). Baylor and Johann-Liang reviewed hepatotoxicity associated with nevirapine use, with their study published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2004 (Volume 35, Issue 5, Pages 538–539). Hitti et al. reported maternal toxicity associated with continuous nevirapine use during pregnancy, based on results from PACTG 1022. The study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2004 (Volume 36, Issue 3, Pages 772–776). Lyons et al. examined maternal hepatotoxicity with nevirapine as part of combination antiretroviral therapy during pregnancy. Their findings were published in HIV Medicine in 2006 (Volume 7, Issue 4, Pages 255–260). Aaron et al. compared adverse events in HIV-infected pregnant and non-pregnant women treated with nevirapine versus non-nevirapine antiretroviral regimens. The study was published in PLoS One in 2010 (Volume 5, Issue 9, e12617).
